PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 72 — Lesson 96: Asthma Management

FNP-level goal: Confirm the asthma pattern, assess current severity and future risk, optimize inhaler-based care and trigger reduction, teach technique and action planning, and recognize exacerbations unsafe for outpatient management.

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish suspected asthma from alternative causes of cough, wheeze, and dyspnea.
  • Assess symptom control, exacerbation history, reliever use, night symptoms, activity limitation, technique, adherence, and triggers.
  • Use current guideline-based controller/reliever strategy with patient-specific safety and access assessment.
  • Recognize severe exacerbation and respiratory-failure red flags.
  • Create a written action plan, follow-up plan, and referral pathway.

Part 1 — Confirm the Pattern and Consider Mimics

Asthma commonly produces variable respiratory symptoms and variable airflow limitation, but cough or wheeze alone is not enough to assume asthma. Consider infection, COPD, heart failure, pulmonary embolism, upper-airway disease, aspiration, medication effects, vocal-cord dysfunction, and other causes when presentation, age, risk factors, or response does not fit. Use appropriate objective testing and current guidance when the patient is stable enough for it.

Part 2 — Control Today and Risk Tomorrow

Assess daytime symptoms, nighttime awakening, reliever use, activity limitation, missed work/school, urgent visits, prior systemic steroid exposure, hospitalization/intubation, smoking/vaping, allergens/occupational exposures, comorbid rhinitis, obesity, reflux, sleep problems, mental health, and medication access. Current symptoms and future exacerbation risk are different domains: a patient may feel well today yet have high future risk after recent severe exacerbations or poor controller access.

Part 3 — Inhalers Work Only When Used Correctly

Before stepping therapy up, verify diagnosis, inhaler technique, adherence, refill access, device preference, and trigger exposure. Ask the patient to demonstrate the device. Review spacer use when appropriate, priming/cleaning, dose tracking, and the difference between controller and reliever medicines. A prescription does not prove medication is being taken or delivered effectively.

Part 4 — Exacerbation Triage

Assess ability to speak, work of breathing, respiratory rate, oxygenation when available, mental status, chest tightness, reliever response, peak-flow data when appropriate, and trajectory. Severe dyspnea, inability to speak in full sentences, cyanosis, exhaustion, altered mental status, silent chest, poor response to reliever, or worsening symptoms despite treatment require emergency evaluation. Do not manage a potentially severe flare through a delayed portal message.

Part 5 — Action Plan and Follow-Up

Provide an accessible written action plan using the patient’s medicines and symptoms: routine daily care, early worsening, emergency symptoms, how to access help, and follow-up. Reassess after treatment changes and exacerbations. Consider pulmonary/allergy or other specialty input for uncertain diagnosis, repeated exacerbations, difficult control, high systemic-steroid burden, occupational concern, or suspected alternative disease.

Clinical Case

A 29-year-old has nighttime symptoms twice weekly, frequent reliever use, two urgent visits this year, and says the controller is “not working.” They demonstrate an incorrect inhaler technique and cannot afford monthly refills.

FNP reasoning: assess current stability, technique, adherence, access, triggers, comorbidities, and exacerbation history before labeling treatment failure. Correct technique, choose an accessible evidence-informed strategy, give an action plan, and arrange timely follow-up.

FNP Asthma Framework

  1. Assess urgency: physiology, work of breathing, response, and emergency red flags.
  2. Confirm/reevaluate diagnosis: variable pattern, objective testing, and mimics.
  3. Measure control and future risk.
  4. Optimize treatment: guideline strategy, technique, adherence, access, and triggers.
  5. Close the loop: written action plan, follow-up, referral, and escalation precautions.

High-Yield Summary

Asthma management: requires diagnosis confirmation, control assessment, future-risk reduction, and inhaler education.
Before escalation: check technique, adherence, access, triggers, and mimics.
Emergency signs: severe distress, poor speech, cyanosis, exhaustion, altered mentation, silent chest, or poor response.
FNP standard: make the plan understandable, accessible, monitored, and safe during worsening symptoms.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Asthma diagnosis, testing, medication strategy, steroid use, action plans, referral, and emergency disposition must follow current guidelines, policy, scope, and the individual patient’s presentation.
